%--------------------------------------
%  Font Settings
%--------------------------------------

\setbeamerfont{structure}{family=\sffamily,series=\mdseries}

\setbeamerfont{title}{size=\LARGE,series=\bfseries,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{subtitle}{size=\normalsize,parent=title}

\setbeamerfont{date}{size=\scriptsize,series=\mdseries,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{author}{size=\large,series=\mdseries,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{institute}{size=\scriptsize,series=\mdseries,parent=structure}

\setbeamerfont{section in toc}{size=\large,series=\bfseries,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{section in head/foot}{size=\tiny,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{subsection in toc}{size=\small,series=\mdseries,parent={section in toc}}

\setbeamerfont{frametitle}{size=\Large,series=\bfseries,parent=structure}
\setbeamerfont{framesubtitle}{parent=frametitle,size=\large}

\setbeamerfont{caption}{size=\footnotesize}
\setbeamerfont{item}{parent=structure,series=\mdseries}
\setbeamerfont{block title}{size=\large,series=\mdseries,parent={structure,block body}}
%-------------------------------------------------------------
%  Package: beamertheme-SimplePlus
%  Author: Pin-Yen Huang (pyhuang97@gmail.com)
%  Version: 1.1, 2025-01-07
%  Link: https://github.com/pm25/SimplePlus-BeamerTheme
%  This is free and unencumbered software released into the
%  public domain; see <http://unlicense.org> for details.
%-------------------------------------------------------------

%--------------------------------------
%  Color Settings
%--------------------------------------

% define custom colors
\definecolor{MutedRed}{rgb}{0.97, 0.92, 0.92}
\definecolor{MutedGreen}{rgb}{0.92, 0.97, 0.92}
\definecolor{MutedBlue}{rgb}{0.92, 0.92, 0.97}
\definecolor{MutedBlack}{rgb}{0.95, 0.95, 0.95}

\definecolor{MediumRed}{rgb}{0.925, 0.345, 0.345}
\definecolor{MediumGreen}{rgb}{0.37, 0.7, 0.66}
\definecolor{MediumBlue}{rgb}{0.015, 0.315, 0.45}
\definecolor{MediumBlack}{rgb}{0.219, 0.259, 0.349}

\definecolor{DarkBlue}{rgb}{0.05, 0.15, 0.35}

% set beamer color themes
\usecolortheme[named=DarkBlue]{structure}

% customize colors for elements
\setbeamercolor{titlelike}{parent=structure}
\setbeamercolor{block title}{fg=white,bg=MediumBlue}
\setbeamercolor{block body}{fg=black,bg=MutedBlue}
\setbeamercolor{block title example}{fg=white,bg=MediumGreen}
\setbeamercolor{block body example}{fg=black,bg=MutedGreen}
\setbeamercolor{block title alerted}{fg=white,bg=MediumRed}
\setbeamercolor{block body alerted}{fg=black,bg=MutedRed}
%-------------------------------------------------------------
%  Package: beamertheme-SimplePlus
%  Author: Pin-Yen Huang (pyhuang97@gmail.com)
%  Version: 1.1, 2025-01-07
%  Link: https://github.com/pm25/SimplePlus-BeamerTheme
%  This is free and unencumbered software released into the
%  public domain; see <http://unlicense.org> for details.
%-------------------------------------------------------------

%--------------------------------------
%  Inner Theme Settings
%--------------------------------------

\pgfdeclareverticalshading[lower.bg,upper.bg]{bmb@transition}{200cm}{%
color(0pt)=(lower.bg); color(2pt)=(lower.bg); color(4pt)=(lower.bg)}

\setbeamersize{text margin left=2em,text margin right=2em}

\setbeamertemplate{footline}[frame number]
\setbeamertemplate{navigation symbols}{}

\setbeamertemplate{blocks}[rounded][shadow=false]

\setbeamertemplate{enumerate items}[default]
\setbeamertemplate{enumerate subitem}[default]
\setbeamertemplate{itemize items}[circle]
\setbeamertemplate{itemize subitem}[circle]

% table of contents (overview) settings
\setbeamertemplate{section in toc}[sections numbered]
\setbeamertemplate{subsection in toc}{%
    \leavevmode
    \leftskip=3.2em
    \rlap{\hskip-2em\inserttocsectionnumber.\inserttocsubsectionnumber}
    \inserttocsubsection\par
}

% frame title customization
\setbeamertemplate{frametitle}{%
    \vspace*{0.5em}
    \bfseries\insertframetitle\par
    \vskip-6pt
    \hrulefill\vspace{-0.1em}
}

% title page customization
\setbeamertemplate{title page}{%
    \vspace{6em}
    \begingroup
    \centering
    % ------------------------
    \begin{beamercolorbox}[sep=10pt,center]{title}
        \usebeamerfont{title}\inserttitle\par%
        \ifx\insertsubtitle\@empty%
        \else%
        \vskip0.25em%
        {\usebeamerfont{subtitle}\usebeamercolor[fg]{subtitle}\insertsubtitle\par}%
        \fi%
    \end{beamercolorbox}%
    \vskip0.5em\par
    % ------------------------
    \begin{beamercolorbox}[sep=8pt,center]{author}
        \usebeamerfont{author}\insertauthor
    \end{beamercolorbox}
    \vskip-1em
    % ------------------------
    \begin{beamercolorbox}[sep=8pt,center]{institute}
        \usebeamerfont{institute}\insertinstitute
    \end{beamercolorbox}
    % ------------------------
    \begin{beamercolorbox}[sep=8pt,center]{date}
        \usebeamerfont{date}\insertdate
    \end{beamercolorbox}\vskip0.5em
    % ------------------------
    {\usebeamercolor[fg]{titlegraphic}\inserttitlegraphic\par}
    \endgroup
    \vfill
}
\makeatother
\setbeameroption{hide notes}

\begin{frame}[t]
\frametitle{Glossary: Microwave Links}
\textbf{Commercial microwave link (CML).}

\vspace{1mm}
A fixed wireless connection between two antennas, used for communications backhaul. In this talk, a link is represented by a line segment $\ell$.

\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{Frequency.}

\vspace{1mm}
The carrier frequency of the microwave signal, measured in GHz.

\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{Polarization.}

\vspace{1mm}
The orientation of the electric field of the microwave signal.
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[t]
\frametitle{Glossary: Rain Field and Attenuation}
\textbf{Rain field.}

\vspace{1mm}
A function from a geographic area $\Omega$ to nonnegative rain rates:
\[R:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R_{\geq0}.\]
For a pixel $s\in\Omega$, $R(s)$ is the rain rate, measured in mm/h.

\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{Rain-induced attenuation.}

\vspace{1mm}
Raindrops absorb and scatter microwave energy, weakening the received signal. Rain-induced attenuation is the additional signal loss along a link, measured in dB.

\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{Specific attenuation.} Signal loss per unit distance, measured in dB/km.
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[t]
\frametitle{Glossary: Forward Model}
\textbf{Forward model.}

\vspace{1mm}
A known function that maps the hidden object to predicted measurements:
\[\text{object}\longrightarrow\text{measurements}.\]
\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{In our case.}

\vspace{1mm}
The hidden object is the rain field $R$. The measurements are the link attenuations:
\[R\longrightarrow\{A_\ell\}_\ell.\]
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[t]
\frametitle{Glossary: Inverse Problem}
\textbf{Inverse problem.}

\vspace{1mm}
Estimate the hidden object from its measurements:
\[\text{measurements}\longrightarrow\text{estimated object}.\]
\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{In our case.}

\vspace{1mm}
Given link attenuations and link properties, estimate the rain field:
\[\{A_\ell\}_\ell\longrightarrow\hat R.\]
\vspace{3mm}
\textbf{Ground truth and reconstruction.}

\vspace{1mm}
The benchmark reference field is $R$. An algorithm returns a reconstruction $\hat R$.
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[t]
\frametitle{Glossary: Evaluation Metrics}
Let $R_i$ and $\hat R_i$ be the reference and reconstructed rain rates at pixel $i$, for $n$ paired pixels.
\[\mathrm{Bias}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat R_i-R_i)\qquad\text{\footnotesize mean signed error}\]
\[\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat R_i-R_i)^2}\qquad\text{\footnotesize root mean squared error}\]
Both metrics have units of mm/h. Positive bias means overestimation.

\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Pearson correlation.} Spatial linear association between the centered maps:
\[\rho=\frac{\sum_i(\hat R_i-\bar{\hat R})(R_i-\bar R)}{\sqrt{\sum_i(\hat R_i-\bar{\hat R})^2}\sqrt{\sum_i(R_i-\bar R)^2}}.\]
\end{frame}

Explain the illustrations from left to right: the antenna scans and emits microwave pulses; raindrops scatter energy and a fraction returns as an echo; return delay locates the scattering volume, while corrected echo power supports an estimate of reflectivity. The wavelength illustration supplies context for scattering. Drop-size distribution affects reflectivity and its conversion to rain rate. Reflectivity is not simply raw returned power. \begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{Milestones in microwave rainfall sensing}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.16\textwidth}p{0.79\textwidth}@{}}
\textbf{1977--1978} & \textbf{Atlas \& Ulbrich; Olsen et al.}\newline
Physical basis: near-linearity at selected frequencies and power-law models.\\
\textbf{1991} & \textbf{Giuli et al.}\newline
Tomographic rainfall-field reconstruction from simulated link attenuations.\\
\textbf{2000--2003} & \textbf{Holt et al.; Rahimi et al.}\newline
Dedicated dual-frequency links: path rainfall compared with gauges and radar.\\
\textbf{2006--2007} & \textbf{Messer et al.; Leijnse et al.}\newline
Rainfall retrieval from commercial links in Israel and the Netherlands.\\
\textbf{2013 / 2016} & \textbf{Overeem et al.}\newline
Netherlands-wide maps using ordinary kriging; later, 2.5 years of maps.\\
\textbf{2020} & \textbf{Graf et al.}\newline
German-wide evaluation with approximately 4,000 CMLs and IDW.\\
\end{tabular}
\par\vspace{3mm}
Our comparison uses IDW, an established baseline in large-scale CML rainfall mapping.
\note{Optional background slide, retained from version 13. These are selected milestones, not a complete history. Dedicated experimental links are distinct from opportunistic sensing with an existing commercial network. Atlas and Ulbrich demonstrated near-linearity under selected frequency and microphysical conditions, not a universal linear relationship. Olsen and colleagues assessed power-law approximations using Mie calculations and experimental comparisons; their tables should not be equated with modern polarization-dependent ITU coefficients. Giuli used simulated observations and recursive tomographic reconstruction; the exact objective and common-frequency assumptions remain unverified. Rahimi et al. (2003) used an approximately linear relation between dual-frequency attenuation differences and path-average rainfall, not simply direct Olsen inversion. Messer (2006) and Leijnse (2007) demonstrated commercial-link rainfall retrieval rather than a validated nationwide mapping product. Overeem (2013) used approximately 2,400 links; the 2016 study produced 15-minute maps over 2.5 years using an average of 3,383 directional links on 2,044 paths. Graf (2020) used approximately 4,000 German links and IDW. IDW and kriging predate these studies. Sources: Atlas and Ulbrich, doi:10.1175/1520-0450(1977)016<1322:PAAIRM>2.0.CO;2; Olsen et al., doi:10.1109/TAP.1978.1141845; Giuli et al., doi:10.1175/1520-0450(1991)030<1323:TRORFT>2.0.CO;2; Rahimi et al., doi:10.1029/2002JD003202; Messer et al., doi:10.1126/science.1120034; Leijnse et al., doi:10.1029/2006WR005631; Overeem et al., doi:10.1073/pnas.1217961110 and doi:10.1002/2016WR019412; Graf et al., https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/24/2931/2020/.}
\end{frame}

The decreasing wave amplitude schematically represents signal attenuation, not a cable, a changed carrier frequency, or a broken connection. The drawing is not to scale. \begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{The rain-attenuation forward model}
\textbf{Specific attenuation}
\[\gamma_\ell(R)=\kappa_\ell R^{\alpha_\ell}\qquad[\mathrm{dB/km}].\]
\textbf{Attenuation along a link}
\[A_\ell(R)=\int_\ell\kappa_\ell R(s)^{\alpha_\ell}\,ds
=\sum_{p\in\mathcal C(\ell)}d_{\ell,p}\kappa_\ell R_p^{\alpha_\ell}.\]
\vspace{2mm}
$d_{\ell,p}$: crossed length in pixel $p$, in km.\par
$R_p$: rain rate in mm/h.\par
Frequency and polarization determine $\kappa_\ell$ and $\alpha_\ell$.
\note{ITU-R P.838-3 power law. The discrete expression assumes a constant rain rate within each computational pixel. Attenuation is rain-induced loss in dB, distinguished from total path loss. Inverting average specific attenuation gives a uniform rain equivalent, not generally the arithmetic path-average rainfall.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{Reference fields and synthetic measurements}
\textbf{Refinement and smoothing}\par
Each 2-km cell becomes $16\times16$ inherited subpixels, at 125-m spacing.
\[R^\star=K_\sigma*R^\uparrow,\qquad
K_\sigma(i,j)=\frac{\exp[-(i^2+j^2)/(2\sigma^2)]}
{\sum_{a,b=-3}^{3}\exp[-(a^2+b^2)/(2\sigma^2)]},\quad\sigma=1.\]
\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Synthetic attenuation}\par
Overlay the network template and apply the rain-attenuation model to $R^\star$.
\vspace{3mm}
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule Statistic & Value (mm/h)\\\midrule
Mean of the 100 spatial patch means & To be computed\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
\note{Kernel indices i,j are -3 to 3. Boundary padding uses nearest values. Smoothing is numerical refinement, not a claim of 125-m radar resolution. The intensity statistic includes dry pixels and gives equal weight to each patch. Winter precipitation may include snow. The synthetic experiment treats reference water-equivalent precipitation as liquid rain for attenuation simulation, which does not validate snow attenuation retrieval.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{Reconstruction methods}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.25\textwidth}p{0.68\textwidth}}
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Main idea}\\\hline
IDW & Treat each link midpoint as a virtual rain gauge.\\
ILDW & Weight observations by distance to the link segment.\\
Regularized optimization & Estimate nonnegative pixel rain rates using attenuation agreement, smoothness, and shrinkage.\\
\end{tabular}
\[\min_{r\geq0}\ \alpha_{\rm atten}J_{\rm atten}(r)
+\alpha_{1d}J_{1d}(r)+\alpha_{2d}J_{2d}(r)+\alpha_{\rm total}J_{\rm total}(r).\]
\note{Source: thesis reconstruction methodology. Weights normalize terms using the ILDW reconstruction. J_total is squared L2 shrinkage, not simply the sum of rain rates. Detailed weight definitions and initialization variants will follow in subsequent revisions.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{A counterexample to convexity}
\small
One horizontal link crosses the middle row of a $3\times3$ grid.
\[R^{(L)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\20&1&1\\1&1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
R^{(R)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1&20\\1&1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
R^{(M)}=\frac{R^{(L)}+R^{(R)}}2.\]
Both endpoint fields produce $A_{\rm obs}=0.80155$ dB.
\[J_{\rm atten}(R)=\frac{(\widehat A(R)-A_{\rm obs})^2}{|\ell|},\qquad
J_{\rm atten}(R^{(L)})=J_{\rm atten}(R^{(R)})=0.\]
For $0<\alpha<1$, strict concavity gives $2(10.5)^\alpha>20^\alpha+1$.
\[J_{\rm atten}(R^{(M)})=0.0050431>\frac{J_{\rm atten}(R^{(L)})+J_{\rm atten}(R^{(R)})}{2}=0.\]
\note{Exact example supplied by the user: 38.003 GHz, horizontal polarization, kappa=0.400171594750, alpha=0.881535333268, d_p=0.125 km for each crossed pixel, link length=0.375 km. Midpoint attenuation=0.845082934781 dB. This proves nonconvexity of the attenuation term for this instance. It does not automatically prove nonconvexity of every possible fully regularized objective.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{Convex surrogate using virtual links}
Replace each link by a virtual observation with the same geometry and a linear attenuation model.
\[R_\ell^{\rm eq}=\left(\frac{A_\ell}{\kappa_\ell|\ell|}\right)^{1/\alpha_\ell},
\qquad A_\ell^0=\kappa_0R_\ell^{\rm eq}|\ell|.\]
\[\widehat A_\ell^0(r)=\kappa_0\sum_p d_{\ell,p}r_p.\]
\vspace{2mm}
The squared residuals are convex in $r$.
Positive squared $\ell_2$ shrinkage makes the surrogate strictly convex.
\vspace{3mm}
Homotopy continuation gradually returns to the original link frequencies.
\note{Adapted from adviser source and thesis. The virtual model sets the attenuation exponent to one. A near-25-GHz reference motivates it, but exact linearity comes from that modeling choice. R_eq is a uniform rain equivalent. Strict convexity requires a positive shrinkage coefficient. Homotopy does not guarantee the global optimum of the final nonconvex objective.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t]
\slidetitle{Conclusions and outlook}
\textbf{Controlled benchmark}\par
Optimization improves mean RMSE and spatial correlation relative to IDW.
\vspace{4mm}
\textbf{Operational validation}\par
Test measured attenuation, baseline estimation, wet-antenna effects, and measurement noise.
\vspace{4mm}
\textbf{Temporal reconstruction and nowcasting}\par
Use optical flow to forecast a reconstructed field, then revise it when new measurements arrive.
\vspace{4mm}
\textbf{Learned rainfall priors}\par
Explore Bayesian reconstruction with a learned prior:
\[p(R\mid A)\propto p(A\mid R)\,p(R).\]
\note{Outlook, not completed experiments. A diffusion model can represent a learned rainfall prior. The likelihood must reflect the attenuation forward model and measurement-error assumptions. Specific diffusion-paper comparisons require verification before attribution. Bayes' posterior is proportional, not inversely proportional, to likelihood times prior.}
\end{frame}
